title: Writing a Useful Review Note for a Rejected Product Cutout
description: Describe a product cutout defect with a file reference, viewing condition, visible evidence and a repeatable acceptance check.
content:
A rejected product image is easier to correct when the reviewer describes what changed and where the problem appears. A message such as “the cutout looks wrong” leaves the editor guessing. A useful review note identifies the file, the viewing condition, the affected detail and the decision needed before the image can be used.

## Identify the exact export

Start with the file name and the product variant shown in the image. Keep the untouched source and the submitted export together so another person can repeat the comparison. If several exports share a similar name, give the reviewer a direct reference to the version under discussion instead of assuming everyone has the newest copy.

The note should distinguish the source photograph from the edited asset. A clipped package corner visible in both files requires a different correction from a corner that disappeared only after masking. Record the comparison before deciding which tool or editing step caused the issue.

## Describe the viewing condition

Explain where you noticed the problem: an editor preview, the exported file in another viewer, a product grid or the full product page. Mention the background used during inspection. A pale fringe can disappear on a white surface and become obvious on charcoal; the same export can therefore lead two reviewers to different conclusions.

For a background-removal workflow, [RemovePhotoBG](https://removephotobg.com/) can be used before this review. Keep the original photograph and evaluate the resulting cutout on the intended destination background. Record the defect you can observe rather than assuming the whole image needs to be processed again.

## Name a visible defect

Use a location that another person can find: the left handle gap, the upper edge of the package or the shadow below the base. Describe the visible result in ordinary language. “A strip of the old white background remains inside the handle” is more actionable than “clean up the image.”

Separate observations from proposed solutions. You may suspect that the mask is too tight, but the important evidence is the missing portion of the rim compared with the original. Allow the editor to choose a correction that preserves the real product detail instead of enforcing an unnecessary technique.

## State what an acceptable correction looks like

Connect the request to the destination. A catalog thumbnail needs the product to remain recognizable; a detail view may need lettering to stay readable. A background change should not alter the variant, reshape the package or turn an opaque label transparent.

Avoid requesting an artificially perfect outline where the original contains hair, translucent material or natural softness. Ask for a comparison with the source and a check at the actual display size. If the source lacks a needed detail, record that limitation and consider another photograph rather than asking an editor to invent it.

## Close the review with a repeatable check

After the correction, reopen the delivered export and repeat the viewing conditions from the original note. Confirm that the named defect has been addressed and that neighboring details have not been damaged. Preview the uploaded version too, because another crop or compression step can change the result.

Keep the final decision alongside the file reference. A short record of the observation, correction and accepted export helps the next reviewer understand why the image is ready. It also prevents an old rejected version from being reintroduced when a catalog is reorganized.
